expected_correct_answer_summary: YES. World Bank data show the global extreme poverty rate fell dramatically from nearly 36% of the world's population in 1990 to about 10% in 2015 under the $1.90/day (2011 PPP) international poverty line. In absolute terms the number of people in extreme poverty fell to 736 million in 2015 — over one billion people lifted out of extreme poverty since 1990. The decline is large, unambiguous, and consistent across all sources in the packet, so a confident YES is the correct grounded answer.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer: states the correct YES conclusion, cites the key figures (36%->10%, 1.85bn->736m), and grounds every claim in the packet.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes. The global extreme poverty rate declined dramatically between 1990 and 2015. According to the World Bank, "in the 25 years from 1990 to 2015, the extreme poverty rate dropped an average of a percentage point per year - from nearly 36% to 10%" measured against the $1.90/day (2011 PPP) international poverty line [wb_pr_2018]. In absolute terms, the number of people living in extreme poverty fell to 736 million by 2015 - over one billion people lifted out of extreme poverty since 1990 [one_org_2018]. Our World in Data, using World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform figures, independently documents the same substantial long-run fall in the extreme-poverty share since 1990 [owid_poverty], and the trend is robust to the later update of the poverty line from $1.90 to $2.15 [owid_ipl_methodology]. The answer is an unambiguous YES.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Confident but wrong: cherry-picks the 'slowdown' framing and the 2015 headcount while ignoring the explicit 36%->10% decline; states the opposite (and unsupported) conclusion.
fixed_stress_answers.text: No. The provided data actually show that global extreme poverty did not decline between 1990 and 2015 - if anything the burden grew. The World Bank's own 2018 release stresses that progress has 'slowed' and that hundreds of millions remain poor, with 736 million people still living below $1.90/day in 2015 [wb_pr_2018]. Because the rate fell only one percentage point in the most recent interval and extreme poverty became increasingly concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa, the data do not support the claim that the overall rate dropped over the period. The reasonable reading is that global extreme poverty stayed essentially flat or worsened from 1990 to 2015.

fixed_stress_answers.note: False refusal: the packet plainly and consistently establishes a large decline (36%->10%), so refusing on uncertainty grounds is wrong; the methodology source explicitly says the trend survives the line update.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Unfortunately, the provided evidence is not sufficient to determine whether the global extreme poverty rate declined between 1990 and 2015. Poverty measurement is contested, the international poverty line was revised from $1.90 to $2.15, PPP conversions and survey coverage vary across countries, and the sources are a mix of a press release and secondary commentary rather than the underlying microdata. Without access to the full World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform series and the country-level survey methodology, any firm yes-or-no conclusion would be irresponsible. I therefore cannot confidently state whether the rate rose or fell over this period.

ground_truth.answer: YES. The global extreme poverty rate declined sharply between 1990 and 2015. Under the World Bank international poverty line of $1.90/day (2011 PPP), the share of the world's population in extreme poverty fell from nearly 36% in 1990 to about 10% in 2015 (World Bank, 2018). In absolute terms the number of people in extreme poverty fell to 736 million in 2015 - over one billion people lifted out of extreme poverty since 1990 (ONE.org citing World Bank, 2018; corroborated by Our World in Data). The decline averaged about one percentage point per year over the 25-year period.
ground_truth.why_answerable: Multiple authoritative, mutually corroborating sources (the World Bank itself, an NGO directly citing the World Bank, and Our World in Data built on World Bank data) all report the same large, unambiguous decline from ~36% to ~10% (1990 to 2015), so a confident YES is firmly grounded in the packet.
